text: The Public Order Ordinance (Cap. 245; Chinese: 公安條例; ’POO’) is primary legislation in Hong Kong that codifies old common law public order offences and imposes notification requirements for public processions and meetings, resembling a licensing regime. It also designates restricted areas along the Hong Kong-China border and in military installations. The 1967 Ordinance was enacted after the 1967 Leftist riots, with the government relying on emergency laws to suppress unrest; the bill was published on 6 October 1967 and passed by the Legislative Council on 15 November 1967. It consolidated prior legislation, including the Peace Preservation Ordinance, the Summary Offences Ordinance, and common law, before the 1967 POO. The 1948 Ordinance, enacted by the British colonial government, transplanted the UK’s Public Order Act 1936 and the Straits Settlements’ binding over procedure and also provided for restricted areas along the Hong Kong-China border. In 1980, the revised POO introduced a licensing system for gatherings in public places. The 1986 Public Order (Amendment) Bill raised concerns about freedom of speech by including a provision that criminalizes publishing "false news" likely to cause alarm or disturb public order, which pro-democrats argued was vaguely defined; this section was repealed in 1989. In 1991, during the final years of colonial rule, the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance (Cap. 383) was enacted, prompting a review of ordinances like the POO that might violate it. In 1995, most provisions of the POO were repealed by the Legislative Council as part of aligning Hong Kong law with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the licensing system was replaced with a simple notification procedure. In October 1996, Democratic Party legislator James To introduced a private member’s bill to remove the Commissioner of Police’s power to control amplification of music or speech; the Secretary for Security, Peter Lai, proposed an amendment specifying that such power would be exercised only if reasonably necessary to prevent an imminent threat to public safety or public order, which was adopted, and the 1996 Amendment Ordinance came into effect on 20 December 1996. The People's Republic of China government viewed the 1995 amendment as maliciously motivated and aimed at reducing the Hong Kong SAR government’s public order powers, claiming it contravened the Hong Kong Basic Law. The Preliminary Working Committee for the HKSAR proposed reinstating the POO, and on 23 February 1997, the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress passed a resolution under Article 160 of the Basic Law to scrap major amendments to the POO. Following this, the Office of the Chief Executive Designate proposed amendments to the POO, the Societies Ordinance, and issued a consultation document titled "Civil Liberty and Social Order" in April 1997, which drew widespread criticism for allegedly restricting civil liberties; the colonial government even issued a commentary criticizing the proposals in an unusual manner. The CE Office scaled back the amendments on 15 May, and the Hong Kong Provisional Legislative Council enacted the new version of the POO on 14 June 1997, which came into force on 1 July 1997. The 1997 amendment granted the government the power to prohibit public meetings or processions on grounds of "national security" and "protection of the rights and freedoms of others," in addition to existing grounds of "public safety" and "public order"; under section 17A, failure to comply is a criminal offence punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment. The current POO defines "public gathering," "public meeting," and "public procession" as activities occurring in a "public place," which is defined under section 2 as any place to which the public or a section of the public are entitled or permitted to access, whether paid or not, and includes places that are or will be used for such meetings as public places. The test for a "public place" is whether access is granted to members of the public or a section thereof (HKSAR v Chau Fung [1998] 4 HKC 652); private premises accessible only to lawful occupiers’ invitees or licensees are not considered public places (Kwok Cheuk Kin v Commissioner of Police); in R v Lam Shing Chow, a fight in a residential flat’s common corridor was not in a public place, but in 香港特別行政區政府 訴 梁超明 [2002] HKCFI 170, the reception area of the Law Society was deemed a public place because the public could enter. Cinemas and racecourses are public places even if entry requires tickets (HKSAR v Pearce [2005] 4 HKC 105 and HKSAR v Chau Fung [1998] 4 HKC 652); areas within a university campus where the public has access are public places, while other school campuses or private areas are not. The first charge under the POO after the handover occurred in 2000 when seven student leaders were arrested for joining an unauthorised demonstration on 26 June 2000 without prior police notification; the protest, seen as civil disobedience, drew public and media sympathy, with over 500 academics signing a petition and about 1,000 people marching without police approval; the Hong Kong Bar Association condemned the police for targeting students, and Secretary for Justice Elsie Leung decided not to prosecute. The first prosecution by the HKSAR government under the notification system was on 9 May 2002 against veteran activist Leung Kwok-hung and two student activists for organising an unauthorised public assembly or assisting in its organisation; on 10 February 2002, Leung organised a procession at Chater Garden without notifying the police, which grew from 40 to about 96 participants and remained peaceful despite repeated police warnings; on 25 November 2002, the three were convicted for organising an unauthorised procession and failing to notify the police, each fined 500 Hong Kong dollars and bound over for three months; Magistrate Partick Li found the notification requirement reasonable for maintaining public order. The appeal was heard at the Court of Final Appeal, where the constitutionality of the notification scheme was challenged; on 8 July 2005, by a 4-to-1 majority, the Court of Final Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the notification system was constitutional, though the vague statutory norm of "ordre public" was severed and replaced with the precise term "public order"; the norm of "protection of the rights and freedoms of others" was deemed too broad and lacking legal certainty; the convictions were affirmed as the severance did not affect them; Justice Bokhary PJ dissented, arguing the entire statutory scheme should be struck down except for the right to notification. The government faced criticism for politically motivated prosecutions, as Leung Kwok-hung was a leader of a radical political group and the student activists were prominent members of the Hong Kong Federation of Students. At the 2005 WTO conference, the Hong Kong Police used the POO to arrest nearly a thousand South Korean farmers, but no one was successfully convicted. In 2011, the HKSAR government recorded 45 prosecutions under the POO, compared to 39 since the handover, with 45 of the 444 protesters arrested mostly involved in three large protests; 54 of the prosecutions were police figures. In 2011, legislators Wong Yuk-man and Albert Chan from the People Power group were convicted for organising and participating in an unlawful assembly after the 1 July protest, where Wong urged supporters to march to Government House, resulting in a sit-down protest on Garden Road that caused significant traffic disruption; sentencing was adjourned until 16 May. On 8 May 2013, Melody Chan, a 26-year-old volunteer of the Occupy Central movement, was arrested for allegedly blocking roads in Central nearly two years earlier, the same protest in which Wong and Chan were previously charged. In the 2016 Mong Kok civil unrest, the government prosecuted 36 protesters with the charge of rioting—a charge previously used only three times since 1970 and carrying a maximum sentence of ten years under the POO—drawing criticism from Hong Kong Watch, which argued the charges of "rioting" and "incitement to riot" were vague and could lead to excessive punishment. The POO is widely criticized as a tool to suppress Hong Kong people’s civil liberties. The Reform Club of Hong Kong opposed the 1967 bill, stating it made every peace-loving resident a potential criminal and that innocent persons without legal representation faced grave risks of conviction. The letter of no objection system has been criticized as a disguised licensing system; strict enforcement would lead to widespread prosecutions, while non-enforcement would render the law a dead letter and violate the rule of law principle.
